newsitem.title: FRANCE: Corsica chief says had secret ties with government.
newsitem.headline: Corsica chief says had secret ties with government.

text.p: A Corsican separatist chief living in hiding said in an interview on Monday that his group had held secret talks with the French government and he named five officials he called its envoys.
Francois Santoni, head of the Cuncolta Naziunalista party, said one of the envoys was Maurice Gourdault-Montagne, a senior aide of Prime Minister Alain Juppe.
His party is a legal front for the outlawed Corsican National Liberation Front (FLNC), Historic Wing, the main hardline separatist group on the French Mediterranean island.

Santoni also told the daily Est-Republicain newspaper that a nightime rally in January of 600 heavily-armed FLNC guerrillas was organised at the behest of the government, wanting to show the French public the group was popular in Corsica and should be negotiated with.
But the rally caused uproar in France, especially since no one one was arrested even though police seemed to know of it.
Juppe's office dismissed Santoni's allegations as "grotesque lies by a terrorist."
"The government has but one policy in Corsica: development of the island, which relies on re-asserting order and thus strictly applying the laws as the population desires," it said in a statement.

French newspapers have long said the centre-right government had had been in contact with the guerrillas in an effort to find a negotiated solution to end a 20-year low-level bombing campaign on the island.
The separatists meanwhile maintained their bombings with an attack against the home of the mayor of the northern town of Bastia early on Monday in defiance of the government crackdown.

The Bastia blast blew out the door of the apartment of Emile Zuccarelli, a former cabinet minister and opposition member of the National Assembly for the small Radical Socialist party.,No one was hurt and Zuccarelli was not at home at the time.
